summary: Describes a lighter form of IP-in-IP tunneling that adds less overhead than the usual method of adding a second full IP header. It reuses information from the original header to save space.

plainLanguage.summary: The big envelope trick wastes paper. This version uses a small sticker with just the new address, so the package stays lighter.

questions: what is minimal encapsulation in ip
how does minimal encapsulation differ from ip in ip
how big is the minimal forwarding header
subtitle: A lighter IP tunnel that inserts a small forwarding header instead of wrapping a whole second IP header.

tldr.problem: Conventional IP-in-IP encapsulation adds a second IP header to every datagram, duplicating several fields in the inner header.
tldr.mechanism: Minimal encapsulation edits the original IP header and inserts an 8 or 12 octet minimal forwarding header that stores the original destination, and optionally the source address, then restores them at the tunnel exit.
tldr.outcome: Tunnels cost fewer bytes per datagram, but the method cannot be used on datagrams that are already fragmented.

today: RFC 2004 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It relies on RFC 2003 for routing-failure, ICMP and security guidance.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Tunnels
sections.content:
RFC 2004 specifies a way to carry an IP datagram as the payload of an IP datagram with less overhead than the conventional method in RFC 2003, which adds a second IP header to each datagram. Encapsulation is a means to alter normal IP routing by delivering a datagram to an intermediate destination that the original Destination Address would not select.

The process is often called tunneling. The encapsulator is the entry point of the tunnel and the decapsulator is the exit point.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel is a shortcut for a package. It goes in at one end, and someone at the other end hands it on to where it was really going.

sections.title: Why a Smaller Encapsulation
sections.content:
The Mobile IP working group specified encapsulation as a way to deliver packets from a mobile node's home network to an agent that can deliver them locally to the mobile node, wherever it is away from home. Other possible uses the RFC lists are multicasting, preferential billing, choice of routes with selected security attributes, and general policy routing.

Using a full IP header to encapsulate duplicates several fields in the inner header. A new mechanism can save space by eliminating that duplication. The scheme comes from earlier Mobile IP Internet Drafts.
sections.plainLanguage: When a friend moves house, mail still goes to the old address and gets forwarded. A forwarding label that repeats less information makes the forwarded parcel lighter.

sections.title: How Encapsulation Works
sections.content:
Use of minimal encapsulation is optional. The minimal forwarding header is inserted after the IP header, followed by the unmodified payload, and no extra IP header is added. The original IP header is modified like this:

  • The Protocol field becomes protocol number 55.
  • The Destination Address becomes the IP address of the tunnel exit point.
  • If the encapsulator is not the original source, the Source Address becomes the encapsulator's address.
  • The Total Length grows by the size of the forwarding header, either 12 or 8 octets depending on the S bit.
  • The Header Checksum is recomputed or updated.

Unlike IP-in-IP encapsulation, the Time to Live is not changed by encapsulation itself. A forwarding encapsulator decrements it through normal forwarding. Because the original TTL stays in the header, hops inside the tunnel are visible to tools such as traceroute.

Decapsulation reverses this. The forwarding header fields are restored to the IP header, the header is removed, Total Length is decremented by its size, and the Header Checksum is recomputed or updated.

The encapsulator may use existing IP mechanisms to deliver to the exit point. IP options are allowed, and fragmentation is allowed unless the Don't Fragment bit is set, so that nodes using Path MTU Discovery can get the information they need.
sections.plainLanguage: Going in, you cross out the address and write the tunnel exit's address, and stick the old one on a note. Coming out, you peel off the note and put the old address back.

sections.title: The Minimal Forwarding Header
sections.content:
The header has a Protocol field, an S bit, a reserved field, a 16-bit Header Checksum, the Original Destination Address, and optionally the Original Source Address.

  • Protocol is copied from the original IP header.
  • S is 0 when the source address is absent, making the header 8 octets, and 1 when present, making it 12 octets.
  • reserved is sent as zero and ignored on reception.
  • Header Checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of all 16-bit words in the minimal forwarding header, computed with the checksum field as 0. The IP header and payload are not included.
  • Original Destination Address is copied from the original header.
  • Original Source Address is copied from the original header and is present only when S is set.

Minimal encapsulation MUST NOT be used when the original datagram is already fragmented, since the header has no room for fragmentation information.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticky note holds the old destination, sometimes the old sender, and a small check number to spot mistakes. It has no space for notes about a parcel that was already split up, so those cannot use it.

sections.title: Routing Failures and ICMP
sections.content: Using any encapsulation for routing makes routing loops more likely. To reduce the danger, a router should follow the procedures in RFC 2003. ICMP messages from within the tunnel are also handled as that RFC specifies, including the maintenance of tunnel soft state.
sections.plainLanguage: Shortcuts can send a package round in circles. This RFC says to follow the same safety rules as the bigger-envelope method.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not address security itself. It says the considerations are generally similar to those in RFC 2003, which defines the conventional IP-in-IP method.
sections.plainLanguage: This note does not add any new safety rules. It points to the ones for the bigger-envelope method.

fields.name: Protocol
fields.desc: Copied from the Protocol field of the original IP header.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: 1 if the Original Source Address is present, which makes the header 12 octets; 0 for 8 octets.

fields.name: reserved
fields.desc: Sent as zero; ignored on reception.

fields.name: Header Checksum
fields.desc: Checksum over the minimal forwarding header only.

fields.name: Original Destination Address
fields.desc: Copied from the original IP header.
